content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) prevention, specifically focusing on TB preventive treatment (TPT). These guidelines, released in 2020, aim to provide updated recommendations based on the latest evidence, particularly regarding shorter rifamycin-containing preventive regimens. The guidelines are designed to improve clarity and global applicability, superseding previous WHO policies on managing latent TB infection (LTBI) in people living with HIV (PLHIV), household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. The guidelines emphasize the importance of TPT as a critical intervention to achieve the End TB Strategy targets, as endorsed by the United Nations High-Level Meeting on TB in 2018. TPT is part of a broader framework of preventive actions, including screening for active TB, infection control, and addressing co-morbidities such as HIV. The recommendations are primarily intended for health ministry staff and policymakers working on TB, HIV, infectious diseases, and maternal and child health. The 2020 update introduces new evidence on shorter preventive regimens, such as a one-month daily rifapentine and isoniazid regimen and a four-month daily rifampicin regimen, as alternative options for TB prevention. These regimens are applicable in all settings, subject to specific conditions. Additionally, the guidelines now include updated advice on isoniazid preventive treatment during pregnancy and the concurrent use of rifapentine and dolutegravir, reflecting findings from recent studies. The guidelines outline 18 key recommendations covering the programmatic management of TPT, including identifying at-risk populations, ruling out active TB, testing for LTBI, providing treatment, and monitoring adherence and adverse events. Notable updates include: 1. Populations for LTBI Testing and TPT: Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TPT as part of comprehensive HIV care, regardless of antiretroviral therapy (ART) status or LTBI testing availability. Infants and children living with HIV who are in contact with TB patients and are unlikely to have active TB should also receive TPT. Household contacts of bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB patients, particularly children under five years, should be given TPT even if LTBI testing is unavailable. 2. Testing for LTBI: Either a tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) can be used to test for LTBI. 3. TPT Options: Recommended regimens include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or three months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. Alternative regimens include one month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone. 4. Special Populations: Systematic LTBI testing and treatment are recommended for individuals initiating anti-TNF treatment, undergoing dialysis, preparing for organ or hematological transplants, or those with silicosis. LTBI testing and treatment may also be considered for prisoners, healthcare workers, immigrants from high TB burden countries, homeless individuals, and people who use drugs. 5. Screening Algorithms: Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered TPT. The guidelines also highlight operational challenges that countries must address to achieve global TB targets. Following the publication of these guidelines, WHO plans to release an operational guide with practical details for implementing the updated recommendations. These documents are part of a modular set of consolidated guidelines and operational guides aimed at streamlining TB prevention efforts worldwide.
